Empirical Research Plan:  “The Causal Effect of Extended Unemployment-Benefit Duration on Unemployment Spells”

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Identification Strategy
Strategy chosen    : Sharp (preferred) or Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD)  
Why it fits      :  
• The Austrian UI schedule creates an age-based discontinuity in potential benefit length that is (i) mechanical, (ii) predetermined, and (iii) verifiable in the data.  
• Age is continuous and essentially impossible for individuals to manipulate.  
• Individuals just below and just above the cut-off are virtually identical except for the length of benefits, satisfying the “as-good-as-random” condition locally.  
• The monthly micro-data give sufficient resolution to implement an RDD with a running variable measured in months (or days).  
If administrative records reveal imperfect compliance (some eligible workers do not claim or some ineligible manage to extend benefits), we will treat it as a Fuzzy RD and instrument actual benefit length with eligibility.  All results are intent-to-treat (ITT) unless otherwise noted.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Treatment and Control

Running variable   : exact age at the start of the unemployment spell, measured in months relative to the statutory birthday cut-off.  
Primary cut-off   : the legal age at which entitlement jumps (e.g., 40th, 45th, 50th birthday).  Multiple cut-offs can be pooled in a “stacked” RD or analysed separately.  

Treatment variable  
• For a sharp RD: TREAT = 1{age ≥ K} where K is the threshold.  
• For a fuzzy RD: BenefitLength (weeks) is the endogenous variable, eligibility is the instrument.  

Control group   : Unemployed individuals whose age at entry falls just below the threshold within an optimally chosen bandwidth h (e.g., ±24 months, to be data-driven).  
Treated group   : Individuals whose age at entry falls just above the same threshold within h.  

Timing     : Assignment is determined at the first month of an unemployment spell; outcome (spell length) is realised afterwards.

Outcome variable  : unemployment_spell_length (weeks or days until exit to employment or censoring).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cut-off  
 Absent the change in benefit duration, expected unemployment length would evolve smoothly in age.  
 Plausibility: labour-market productivity and search effort do not change discretely exactly at age K.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable (age)  
 Plausibility: chronological age cannot be gamed; but timing of job separation relative to birthday could be.  This will be tested with density and “bunching” checks.  

A3. Local randomisation / covariate balance near K  
 Observable characteristics (gender, tenure, previous wages, region, season) should be continuous.  To be tested.  

A4. (Fuzzy RD only) First-stage relevance and monotonicity  
 Eligibility must cause a significant jump in actual benefit length, and no one should receive shorter benefits because of eligibility.  Institutional rules strongly support both.  

A5. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)  
 One individual’s eligibility should not affect another’s unemployment duration within the narrow band.  Market-wide general equilibrium effects are negligible locally.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Threats to Identification & Remedies

T1. Strategic timing of layoffs around birthdays  
 • Conduct McCrary density test; if bunching appears, implement a “donut” RD excluding observations very close to the threshold.  
 • Show robustness to alternative bandwidths and polynomial orders.  

T2. Age-related labour-market programs or retirement options that also change at K  
 • Document all concurrent policies; include indicators for early-retirement eligibility, training programs, etc. and test for discontinuities in them.  
 • If another program jumps, estimate a multi-cutoff RD or control directly for those entitlements.  

T3. Heterogeneous macro conditions across cohorts (1980–1999)  
 • Add year × month fixed effects in the RD regression.  
 • Perform placebo RD at fictitious cut-offs and within subsamples (booms vs recessions).  

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  R Code Outline  (executable)

```r
# ------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # high-dimensional FE
library(rdrobust)       # RDD estimation
library(ggplot2)        # plots
library(rddensity)      # McCrary test

# ------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ------------------------------------------
ui <- fread("austria_ui_1980_1999.csv")   # assumes one row = spell-month

# ------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ------------------------------------------
# Age in months at spell start
ui[, age_months := floor(12*(age_years + age_month_frac))]   # adjust if already in months
cutoff_months <- 40*12                                        # example for age 40

ui[, running := age_months - cutoff_months]                  # 0 = hits 40th birthday
ui[, treat  := (running >= 0)]                               # sharp RD treatment

# Outcome: total spell length in weeks
ui[, spell_len := as.numeric(exit_date - start_date)/7 ]

# Keep one row per spell
spell <- unique(ui, by = "spell_id")

# ------------------------------------------
# 3. Main sharp RD (global polynomial p=1, BW selected by rdrobust)
# ------------------------------------------
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = spell$spell_len,
                    x = spell$running,
                    c = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")

summary(rd_main)

# ------------------------------------------
# 4. Fuzzy RD (if compliance <100%)
# ------------------------------------------
# First verify jump in benefit duration
rd_first <- rdrobust(y = spell$benefit_weeks, x = spell$running, c = 0)
summary(rd_first)      # should show large discontinuity

rd_fuzzy <- rdrobust(y = spell$spell_len,
                     x = spell$running,
                     c = 0,
                     fuzzy = spell$treat)   # eligibility as instrument
summary(rd_fuzzy)

# ------------------------------------------
# 5. Covariate balance & manipulation checks
# ------------------------------------------
# 5a. McCrary density
dens <- rddensity(X = spell$running, c = 0)
summary(dens); plot(dens)

# 5b. Covariate continuity example: prior wage
for (var in c("gender","prior_wage","region","industry")){
   print(rdrobust(y = spell[[var]], x = spell$running, c = 0)$coef)
}

# ------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: alternative bandwidth (±12 months) with fixest
# ------------------------------------------
bw <- 12
sub <- spell[abs(running) <= bw]

reg_alt <- feols(spell_len ~ treat + running + I(running^2), data = sub,
                 weights = ~triangular(abs(running)/bw))
summary(reg_alt)

```

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Expected Results

Economic theory (search models with moral hazard) predicts that more generous benefit duration prolongs job search.  Prior empirical elasticities for European systems range from 0.1–0.3 extra week of unemployment per additional week of entitlement.  
I therefore expect a discrete increase in average spell length of roughly 10–20 %, e.g., an extra 3–5 weeks for a 26-week extension.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)

C1: No manipulation of running variable     1  
C2: Continuity of potential outcomes / covariates 1  
C3: Strong first stage (benefit jump)       1  
C4: Appropriate bandwidth & functional form chosen 1  
C5: Assessment of other simultaneous discontinuities 0.5  

Total 4.5 / 5 → design appears highly credible, subject to passing the density and balance tests.
